The '''Luoshu''' ([[pinyin]]), '''Lo Shu''' ([[Wade-Giles]]), or '''Nine Halls Diagram'''<!--Chinese in infobox per WP:MOS-ZH--> is an [[Ancient China|ancient Chinese]] diagram and named for the [[Luo River (Henan)|Luo River]] near [[Luoyang]], [[Henan]]. The Luoshu appears in [[Chinese mythology|myths]] concerning the [[Chinese inventions|invention]] of [[Chinese writing|writing]] by [[Cangjie]] and other [[culture hero]]es. It is a unique normal [[magic square]] of order three. It is usually paired with the [[Yellow River Map|River Map or Hetu]]{{mdash}}named in reference to the [[Yellow River]]{{mdash}}and used with the River Map in various contexts involving [[Chinese geomancy]], [[Chinese numerology|numerology]], [[Chinese philosophy|philosophy]], and early [[natural science]].

==Traditions==
The Lo Shu is part of the legacy of ancient Chinese mathematical and divination (cf. the [[I Ching]] {{lang|zh|易經}}) traditions, and is an important emblem in ''[[Feng Shui]]'' ({{lang|zh|風水}})—the art of [[geomancy]] concerned with the placement of objects in relation to the flow of [[qi]] ({{lang|zh|氣}}), or "natural energy".{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}}

== History ==
A Chinese legend concerning the pre-historic [[Yu the Great|Emperor Yu]] ({{lang|zh|夏禹}}) tells of the Lo Shu, often in connection with the ''Yellow River Map'' (Hetu) and the [[Bagua (concept)|eight trigrams]]. In ancient China there is a legend of a huge [[Flood myth|deluge]]: the people offered sacrifices to the god of one of the flooding rivers, the Luo river ({{lang|zh|洛河}}), to try to calm his anger.  A magical [[turtle]] emerged from the water with the curiously unnatural Lo Shu pattern on its shell: circular dots representing the integers one through nine are arranged in a three-by-three grid.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Cammann | first = Schuyler
 | date = April–June 1960
 | journal = Journal of the American Oriental Society
 | jstor = 595587
 | pages = 116–124
 | title = The evolution of magic squares in China
 | volume = 80| issue = 2
 | doi = 10.2307/595587
 }}</ref>

Early records dated to 650 BCE are ambiguous, referring to a "river map", but clearly start to refer to a [[magic square]] by 80 CE, and explicitly give an example of one since 570 CE.<ref name="cammann3">{{harvnb|Cammann|1961}}</ref><ref name="Swaney">{{cite web | last=Swaney |first=Mark |title=Mark Swaney on the History of Magic Squares |url=http://www.netmastersinc.com/secrets/magic_squares.htm
| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040807015853/http://www.netmastersinc.com/secrets/magic_squares.htm |archive-date=2004-08-07}}</ref>  Recent publications have provided support that the Lo Shu Magic Square was an important model for time and space.{{Cn|date=July 2024}}  It served as a basis for city planning, and tomb and temple design. The magic square was incidentally used to designate spaces of political and religious importance.<ref>{{harvnb|Schinz|1996}}{{pages needed|date=July 2019}}</ref> 

[[File:Carus-p48-Mystic-table.jpg|thumb|upright=1|The Lo Shu square on the back of a small turtle (in the center), surrounded by the signs of the [[Chinese zodiac]] and the [[Bagua|Eight Trigrams]], are all carried by a large turtle (that presumably stands for the [[Longma|Dragon horse]] that had earlier revealed the trigrams to [[Fu Xi]]).{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}}  This example drawn by an anonymous Tibetan artist.]]

==The layout==
The odd and even numbers alternate in the periphery of the Lo Shu pattern; the four even numbers are at the four corners, and the five odd numbers (which outnumber the even numbers by one) form a cross in the center of the square. The sums in each of the three rows, in each of the three columns, and in both diagonals, are all 15.<ref group=notes name="b">15 is the number of days in each of the 24 cycles of the [[Chinese calendar|Chinese solar year]].</ref>  Since "5" is in the center cell, the sum of any two other cells that are directly through the five from each other must be 10; e.g., opposite squares and corners add up to 10, the number of the ''Yellow River Map''.{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}}

==In numerology==
The Lo Shu is sometimes connected numerologically with the "[[Bagua]]" ({{lang|zh|八卦}} or eight [[trigrams]]"), that can be arranged in the eight outer cells, reminiscent of circular trigram diagrams. Because north is placed at the bottom of maps in China, the 3x3 [[magic square]] having number 1 at the bottom and 9 at the top is used in preference to the other rotations/reflections. As seen in the [[Bagua#King_Wen's_"Later_Heaven"|"Later Heaven"]] arrangement, 1 and 9 correspond with ☵ Kǎn {{lang|zh|坎}} "Water {{lang|zh|水}}" and ☲ Lí {{lang|zh|離}} "Fire {{Lang|zh|火}}" respectively. In the [[Bagua#Fu_Xi's_"Earlier_Heaven"|"Early Heaven"]] arrangement, they would correspond with ☷ Kūn {{lang|zh|坤}} "Earth {{lang|zh|地}}" and ☰ Qián {{lang|zh|乾}} "Heaven {{lang|zh|天}}" respectively. Like the ''Yellow River Map'', the Lo Shu square, in conjunction with the Bagua, is sometimes used as a [[mandala|mandalic]] representation important in Feng Shui geomancy.{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}}
